title: Not my contest
hookLine: you can be unbeatable if you enter no contest where winning isn't up to you (Enchiridion 19)

cards: Late at night, thumb on the screen. An old classmate just bought a house. Someone's kid got into the program.
A coworker is posting from a beach so blue it looks fake. Nobody announced a race. Nobody handed out numbers.
And yet somehow you're running, and losing, at eleven forty on a Tuesday.
Epictetus never saw a phone, but section nineteen of his handbook speaks straight to that race, and it opens with a claim that sounds like a boast: you can be unbeatable.

teach.b: You can be invincible, Epictetus says, if you never enter a contest where winning isn't up to you. The Greek for contest is agon: a match, a bout, a trial of strength. Then the trap.

teach.h: DON'T THINK THE HONORED ARE HAPPY.
teach.b: When you see someone honored above you, or powerful, or admired, he says, watch out that the impression doesn't carry you off into thinking they must be happy.
That's the moment a person signs up for a contest without noticing: their house, their title, their beach, and suddenly you're competitors.
If what's truly good lies in what's up to us, he says, then there's no room for envy or jealousy. You can't envy someone for something that was never the prize.
And then the line: you yourself don't really want to be a general or a magistrate or a consul. You want to be free. And there's only one road to that: to care little for things not in our power.

This isn't a refusal to try at anything. Train for the race, apply for the job, write the book. What Epictetus refuses is to stake your peace on the result, which depends on judges, timing and other people.
The contest where winning is up to you is a different one: patience against your own temper, honesty against your own excuses. You can win that one every day.
So when the scrolling starts a race, you can stand at the line, watch the runners go, and say: not my contest.

how: Some Stoic practitioners notice when they start comparing themselves with others and decline to stake their peace on outcomes that depend on others.

o: a soldier's oath of loyalty to a general
a contest: a match or trial of strength
a Greek law court where cases were judged

games.q: not my contest — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says never try at anything
he says don't stake your peace on a contest where winning isn't up to you.
Epictetus says what you really want is not to be consul, but to be free
and the one road there is caring little for what isn't up to you.
section nineteen says there is no room for envy if the good is in our power
you can't envy someone for what was never the prize.

games.q: a rival has just been honored above you in front of everyone. what does Epictetus warn against?
o: being carried off into thinking they must be happy.
games.why: don't let the impression carry you into thinking them happy; if the good lies in what's up to us, there's nothing to envy.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've compared yourself to lately, and what they have that stings: the title, the house, the ease.
Picture a starting line and the race beginning without you, while you stay where you are and say inside: not my contest.
Then name the contest that is yours today, being patient, being honest, finishing one thing well, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Agon. The Greek word for a contest, a match, a trial of strength; Epictetus says you can be unbeatable if you never enter one where winning isn't up to you. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 19: a contest, a match, a struggle.

carryVoice: Your line: stand at the line. Your own race is the one with no other runners. Day three hundred fifty-one, done.
